paragraphs: “That’s true, Katya,” Mitya roared suddenly. “I looked into your eyes and I knew you were dishonoring me, and I took your money anyway. Despise me as a scoundrel, all of you, despise me! I’ve earned it!”
“Prisoner,” cried the President, “one more word and I will have you removed.”

“That money tormented him,” Katya went on, in a rush. “He wanted to pay it back. He did want to, that’s true. But he needed money for that creature, too. So he murdered his father, and he never paid me back. He went off with her to that village where he was arrested. There he squandered the money he had stolen after killing his father. And the day before the murder he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it. I saw that at once, at the time. He wrote it out of spite, and he was certain, absolutely certain, that I would never show it to anyone, even if he did kill him. Otherwise he wouldn’t have written it. He knew I wouldn’t want revenge and ruin him! But read it, read it carefully, more carefully, please, and you will see that he described everything in his letter, all in advance: how he would kill his father and where the money was kept. Look, please, don’t overlook this. There’s one phrase: ‘I shall kill him as soon as Ivan has gone away.’ So he thought out beforehand how he would kill him,” Katerina Ivanovna pointed out to the court, with venomous, spiteful triumph. Oh, it was clear she had studied every line of that letter and caught every meaning hidden under it. “If he hadn’t been drunk, he wouldn’t have written to me. But look, everything is written there in advance, exactly as he committed the murder afterwards. A complete program of it!” she exclaimed frantically.

She no longer cared about any consequences to herself, though no doubt she had foreseen them even a month ago. Even then, perhaps, shaking with anger, she had weighed whether to show the letter at the trial or not. Now she had taken the fatal plunge. I remember that the letter was read aloud by the clerk, right afterwards, I believe. It made an overwhelming impression. They asked Mitya whether he admitted writing it.

“It’s mine, mine!” cried Mitya. “I’d never have written it sober!... We’ve hated each other for plenty of reasons, Katya, but I swear, I swear, I loved you even while I hated you. And you didn’t love me!”

He sank back onto his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense began cross-examining her. Mostly they wanted to find out what had led her to hide such a document, and to give her evidence in such a different tone and spirit only a short while before.

“Yes, yes. I was lying just now. I lied against my honor and my conscience. But I wanted to save him, because he hates me so, and despises me!” Katya cried madly. “Oh, how horribly he despises me! He always has. Do you know, he has despised me from the very moment I bowed down to him for that money? I saw it.... I felt it right then, but for a long time I refused to believe it. How often I have read it in his eyes: ‘And yet you came of your own accord.’ Oh, he didn’t understand. He had no idea why I ran to him. He can imagine nothing but baseness. He measured me by himself. He thought everyone was like him!” Katya hissed furiously, in a perfect frenzy. “And he only wanted to marry me because I’d come into a fortune. Because of that, because of that! I always suspected it was because of that! Oh, he is a brute! He was always sure that I would tremble with shame in front of him all my life, because I had gone to him that time. He was sure he had the right to despise me forever for it, and so to stand above me. That’s why he wanted to marry me! That’s how it was, that’s all it was! I tried to win him with my love, a love without limits. I even tried to forgive him his unfaithfulness. But he understood nothing, nothing! How could he, really? He is a monster! I only received that letter the next evening. They brought it to me from the tavern. And that very morning, that very morning, I had wanted to forgive him everything, everything, even his treachery!”

The President and the prosecutor, of course, tried to calm her. I can’t help thinking they were ashamed to be taking advantage of her hysteria and listening to such confessions. I remember hearing them say to her, “We understand how hard this is for you; believe us, we can feel for you,” and so on, and so on. And yet they drew the evidence out of the raving, hysterical woman all the same. At last she described how Ivan had been almost driven out of his mind for the past two months, trying to save “the monster and murderer,” his brother. She spoke with that remarkable clearness which so often comes, if only for a moment, in such overwrought states.

“He tortured himself,” she exclaimed. “He was always trying to make his brother’s guilt smaller, and confessing to me that he, too, had never loved his father, and perhaps even wished for his death himself. Oh, he has a tender, too tender, conscience! He tormented himself with his conscience! He told me everything, everything! He came every day and talked to me as his only friend. I have the honor to be his only friend!” she cried suddenly, with a sort of defiance, and her eyes flashed. “He went to see Smerdyakov twice. One day he came to me and said, ‘If it wasn’t my brother but Smerdyakov who committed the murder’ (for the story was going around everywhere that Smerdyakov had done it), ‘perhaps I am guilty too, for Smerdyakov knew I didn’t like my father and perhaps believed I wanted my father dead.’ Then I brought out that letter and showed it to him. He was completely convinced that his brother had done it, and it overwhelmed him. He couldn’t bear the thought that his own brother was a parricide! Only a week ago I saw that it was making him ill. In the last few days he has talked incoherently in my presence. I saw his mind was giving way. He walked about raving. People saw him muttering in the streets. The doctor from Moscow examined him the day before yesterday, at my request, and told me he was on the eve of brain fever. And all on his account, on account of this monster! And last night he learned that Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock that it drove him out of his mind... and all because of this monster, all for the sake of saving the monster!”

Oh, of course, an outpouring like this, a confession like this, is possible only once in a lifetime. At the hour of death, say, on the way to the scaffold! But it was in Katya’s nature, and this was such a moment in her life. This was the same impetuous Katya who had once thrown herself on the mercy of a young profligate to save her father. This was the same Katya who, a little while before, in her pride and chastity, had sacrificed herself and her maidenly modesty in front of all these people. She had told of Mitya’s generous conduct, hoping to soften his fate a little. And now she sacrificed herself again, but this time for someone else. Perhaps only now, only at this moment, did she feel and know how dear that other man was to her! She had sacrificed herself out of terror for him. She had suddenly realized that he had ruined himself by confessing that he, not his brother, had committed the murder. She had sacrificed herself to save him, to save his good name, his reputation!

And yet a terrible doubt crossed one’s mind. Was she lying when she described her old relations with Mitya? That was the question. No, she had not meant to slander him when she cried that Mitya despised her for bowing down to him! She believed it herself. She had been firmly convinced, perhaps ever since that bow, that the simple-hearted Mitya, who even then worshipped her, was laughing at her and despising her. She had loved him with a hysterical, “lacerated” love, out of pride alone, wounded pride, and that love was less like love than like revenge. Oh, perhaps that lacerated love might have grown into real love. Perhaps Katya wanted nothing more than that. But Mitya’s unfaithfulness had wounded her to the depths of her heart, and her heart could not forgive him. The moment of revenge had come suddenly. All that had piled up so long and so painfully in the wronged woman’s breast burst out at once, without warning. She betrayed Mitya, but she betrayed herself as well. And as soon as she had given her feelings full expression, the strain was of course over, and shame overwhelmed her. The hysterics started again. She fell to the floor, sobbing and screaming. She was carried out. At that moment Grushenka, with a wail, rushed toward Mitya before anyone had time to stop her.

“Mitya,” she wailed, “that serpent of yours has destroyed you! See, she has shown you what she is!” she shouted to the judges, shaking with rage. At a signal from the President, men seized her and tried to take her out of the courtroom. She would not let them. She fought and struggled to get back to Mitya. Mitya let out a cry and strained toward her. They overpowered him.

Yes, I think the ladies who had come for the spectacle must have been satisfied. The show had certainly been varied. Next, I remember, the Moscow doctor came in. I believe the President had sent the court usher earlier to arrange medical help for Ivan. The doctor informed the court that the sick man had a dangerous attack of brain fever and had to be taken away at once. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense questioned him. He said the patient had come to see him of his own accord the day before yesterday. He had warned him then that such an attack was coming, but the man had refused to be looked after. “He was certainly not in a normal state of mind. He told me himself that he saw visions while awake, that he met several dead people in the street, and that Satan visited him every evening,” the doctor finished. Having given his evidence, the celebrated doctor left. The letter produced by Katerina Ivanovna was added to the material evidence. After some deliberation, the judges decided to continue the trial and to enter both unexpected pieces of evidence (from Ivan and from Katerina Ivanovna) in the record.

But I will not set down the testimony of the other witnesses. They only repeated and confirmed what had been said already, each in his own characteristic way. I say again, it was all gathered up in the prosecutor’s speech, which I will quote shortly. Everyone was excited, everyone was electrified by the catastrophe we had just seen, and all of them waited with intense impatience for the speeches for the prosecution and the defense. Fetyukovitch was plainly shaken by Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence. The prosecutor, though, was triumphant. When all the evidence had been heard, the court adjourned for almost an hour. I believe it was exactly eight o’clock when the President took his seat again and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his speech.
